facts.fact: The article is dated August 7, 2026 in its published-time metadata.
The article identifies four common approaches SMBs use to track phone calls: static numbers, dedicated tracking numbers, dynamic number insertion, and website-level event tagging.
facts.quote: The four common approaches are static numbers, dedicated tracking numbers, dynamic number insertion, and website-level event tagging.

facts.fact: Call detail records (CDRs) are network-layer records that mobile operators have used for billing and operations for decades.
facts.quote: are network-layer records that mobile operators have used for billing and operations for decades

facts.fact: The article says CDRs include fields such as source and destination numbers, call time, call duration, and the cell-tower equipment involved.
facts.quote: they include fields like the source and destination numbers, call time, call duration, and the cell-tower equipment involved

facts.fact: The article attributes its description of CDR structure to a U.S. Census Bureau methods paper on CDRs.
facts.quote: as described in the U.S. Census Bureau methods paper on CDRs

facts.fact: Dynamic number insertion (DNI) swaps the on-site phone number based on the visitor's traffic source.
facts.quote: goes further by swapping the on-site number based on the visitor’s source

facts.fact: Event-level tracking of tel: link clicks measures intent to call, not an actual connected call, according to the article.
facts.quote: because it measures intent to call, not an actual connected call

facts.fact: The article's launch checklist contains four items, including confirming forwarding, loading the DNI script on every major page, verifying analytics events on tel clicks, and making sure CRM fields capture source and outcome.
facts.quote: Load the DNI script on every major page

facts.fact: Adwave's own platform claims it generates a broadcast-ready ad from a website URL and places it across 100+ premium channels, including NBC, Hulu, and ESPN (vendor claim).
facts.quote: Adwave’s platform generates a broadcast-ready ad from a website URL and places it across 100+ premium channels including NBC, Hulu, and ESPN

facts.fact: The page's ROI formula multiplies qualified calls by conversion rate and average revenue per sale, then compares the result against ad spend and tracking cost.
facts.quote: Take the calls that were qualified, multiply them by your conversion rate and average revenue per sale, then compare that against the ad spend and tracking cost.

facts.fact: The page says call-tracking pricing usually takes one of several forms: per-number, per-minute, per-call, or a platform tier. No specific prices are given.
facts.quote: Call-tracking pricing usually shows up in a few forms, per-number, per-minute, per-call, or as a platform tier.

facts.fact: The page states that if a business records calls, it must handle consent carefully, especially across state lines or where consent rules are stricter.
facts.quote: If a team records calls, it needs to handle consent carefully, especially across state lines or in places with stricter consent rules.

facts.fact: The page states that TV call tracking differs from digital because there is no click trail, form fill, or browser session to connect, so the phone number itself is the signal.
facts.quote: TV call tracking works differently from digital because there’s no click trail, no form fill, and no browser session to stitch together.

facts.fact: The page lists the core call-tracking KPIs as inbound calls, outbound calls, missed calls, answer rate, average call duration, qualified-call rate, and cost per qualified call (if tied to revenue).
facts.quote: The core KPIs are the ones that show both volume and quality.
